body.heading: The water you drink is ancient
paragraphs: Here is a thought to bend your mind: the water in your glass today has been rain, river, ocean and cloud before — possibly in dinosaur times. Earth does not get new water delivered. It recycles the same water forever, in a giant circle called the water cycle. It has four steps.

body.heading: Step 1 and 2: up it goes
paragraphs: Step 1 — Evaporation. The sun heats water in oceans, lakes, puddles — even wet laundry — and turns its surface into invisible vapor that rises into the air. (Plants join in too, breathing vapor out of their leaves.)

Step 2 — Condensation. High up, the air is cold. The vapor cools and gathers into tiny droplets — and droplets gathered by the billion are a cloud. Your bathroom mirror fogging up is condensation doing the same trick at home.

body.heading: Step 3 and 4: down it comes, and gathers
paragraphs: Step 3 — Precipitation. When droplets grow too heavy to float, gravity wins: water falls as rain, snow, sleet or hail.

Step 4 — Collection. Fallen water gathers — in puddles, streams, rivers, lakes, oceans, and deep underground stores. And there it waits until the sun lifts it again. The circle has no start and no finish.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Follow one drop: imagine a raindrop landing on your street. Where has it been in the last year? Where will it be next year?
2. Why do you think the water cycle matters to farmers, sailors and skiers in completely different ways?

takeaway: Water endlessly circles through evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection — the rain on your window is older than the dinosaurs.

screenFreeExtension: Cloud watch: lie on the grass for five minutes and track one cloud. Is it growing (condensing) or thinning (evaporating)?
